title: GOD ASKED MOSES ONE QUESTION THAT COULD CHANGE THE WAY YOU SEE YOUR ENTIRE LIFE: “WHAT IS THAT IN YOUR HAND?”
paragraphs: GOD ASKED MOSES ONE QUESTION THAT COULD CHANGE THE WAY YOU SEE YOUR ENTIRE LIFE: “WHAT IS THAT IN YOUR HAND?”

He wasn't holding a sword. He wasn't carrying a crown. He had no army, no influence, and no reason to believe he was qualified. Just an ordinary shepherd's staff. But what happened next reveals something extraordinary about the God who takes broken people, ordinary things, and impossible situations—and writes stories nobody saw coming.
What if the very thing you've been overlooking is the thing God is about to use?
Read that again.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is staring at a life that looks nothing like the one they prayed for.
Maybe it's you.
You thought you'd be further by now. Stronger in your faith. More secure in your calling. Less haunted by your past.

Instead, you're trying to make peace with disappointments you never expected, carrying responsibilities nobody sees, and quietly wondering whether God can still do anything meaningful with what's left of your life.
You look at other people and see gifts, opportunities, connections, confidence.
Then you look at yourself.
And all you see is an ordinary person with an ordinary life, holding what seems like an ordinary thing.
But there is a question buried in the book of Exodus that might change the way you see everything.
It is only five Hebrew words.
And God asked it of a man who had spent forty years in the wilderness.
“What is that in your hand?” — Exodus 4:2
The answer was simple.
“A staff.”
But the story behind that answer is anything but simple.
Because the man holding that staff was Moses.
And Moses had a past.
Before he became the man who confronted Pharaoh, he was a man who had fled Egypt.
Before he stood before the Red Sea, he had stood over the consequences of his own actions.
Before he became the leader of Israel, he had been a fugitive.
Exodus 2 tells us that Moses killed an Egyptian who was beating a Hebrew. When Pharaoh heard what had happened, he sought to kill Moses, and Moses fled to Midian.
Imagine the weight of that history.

He had grown up in Pharaoh's household, yet he was born among the enslaved Hebrews. He had seen oppression. He had acted violently. And now the man who once lived near the center of Egyptian power was tending sheep in a foreign land.
The Bible doesn't tell us everything Moses felt during those wilderness years.
But it tells us enough to know that his life had changed dramatically.
Forty years passed between his flight from Egypt and the calling described in Exodus 3 and 4, as Acts 7:23–30 recounts.
Forty years.
That's enough time for youthful dreams to become distant memories.
Enough time for a man to become accustomed to a different life.
Enough time to wonder whether the story he once imagined was already over.
Then, one day, while Moses was tending the flock of Jethro, his father-in-law, he came to Horeb, the mountain of God.
And there, a bush burned.
But it was not consumed.
Moses turned aside to look.
And God called him by name.
“Moses, Moses.”
Suddenly, the wilderness was no longer merely the place where Moses worked.
It became the place where God spoke.
And what God said was astonishing.
He had seen the affliction of His people in Egypt. He had heard their cry. He knew their suffering. And He was sending Moses to Pharaoh to bring the Israelites out of bondage.
Think about that.
The man who had fled Pharaoh was being sent back to confront Pharaoh.
The man who had spent decades caring for sheep was being called to lead a nation.
The man who knew his limitations was being given an assignment far greater than his natural ability.
And Moses did not respond with the confidence we might expect from a future deliverer.
He questioned his adequacy.
“Who am I, that I should go unto Pharaoh?” (Exodus 3:11, KJV)
Then he worried about what he should say.
Then he worried that the Israelites would not believe him.
And later, he protested that he was not eloquent.
Finally, he pleaded for God to send someone else.
Does that sound familiar?
Maybe you've never stood before a burning bush.
Maybe you've never been called to confront a king.
But you know what it feels like to hear a responsibility pressing against your heart while your insecurities start listing every reason you cannot possibly fulfill it.
“I'm not ready.”
“I'm not educated enough.”
“I'm too old.”
“I'm too young.”
“I've made too many mistakes.”
“Someone else could do it better.”
“God, You know my past.”
And perhaps the most painful one:
“Lord, why would You choose someone like me?”
But notice something remarkable.
When Moses asked, “Who am I?” God did not begin by telling Moses how extraordinary Moses was.
He answered:
“Certainly I will be with thee.” — Exodus 3:12, KJV
That is where the story begins to change.
Not with Moses discovering that he was secretly powerful.
But with Moses learning that the living God would be with him.
God did not promise that Moses would suddenly become self-sufficient.
He promised His presence.
And that distinction matters.
Because much of what we call confidence is built on what we believe we can accomplish.
Biblical faith rests on the character, promises, and power of God.
Then came the question.
The one that seems almost too ordinary for such an extraordinary moment.
In Exodus 4:2, the Hebrew text reads:
מַה־זֶּה בְיָדֶךָ
Mah-zeh veyadekha?
“What is that in your hand?”
Moses answered:
מַטֶּה
Matteh.
“A staff.”
The Hebrew word matteh can refer to a staff or rod. In this setting, it was the staff Moses had in his hand as a shepherd.
Not a royal scepter.
Not a weapon forged for war.
Not some treasure from Pharaoh's palace.
A staff.
Something familiar.
Something ordinary.
Something he could carry into the wilderness every day without expecting anyone to be impressed.
And here is what makes the question so profound.
God was not asking because He lacked information.
The God who had seen Israel's suffering, heard their cries, and revealed Himself to Moses did not need Moses to identify an object for Him.
The question draws attention to what Moses already possesses, just before God reveals what He can do with it.
And that should make us think.
How often do we ask God to give us something impressive before we are willing to obey Him?
A bigger platform.
More money.
More influence.
A perfect past.
An extraordinary talent.
A life without complications.
Yet here was Moses, holding a simple shepherd's staff.
And God said:
“Cast it on the ground.”
So Moses threw it down.
And it became a serpent.
Moses fled from it.
Let that moment settle.
The man who would eventually stand before Pharaoh was frightened enough to run from the sign God had just performed.
The Bible doesn't hide that detail.
Moses was not portrayed as a fearless superhero.
He was a real man encountering the terrifying power of a holy God.
Then God commanded him to reach out and take the serpent by the tail.
Moses obeyed.
And it became a staff again in his hand.
The Lord explained that the sign would help establish that the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob had appeared to Moses.
That is the context.
The miracle was not a lesson in discovering magical abilities hidden inside an everyday object.
It was a sign of God's authority, given to authenticate His messenger.
The staff itself was not divine.
Moses did not possess supernatural power independently of God.
And this passage does not promise that every ordinary possession will become an instrument of miracles.
The power was never in the wood. The power belonged to the God who commanded Moses to use it.
Please don't miss that.
Because there is a dangerous way to read this story.
We can turn it into a message that says, “You already have everything you need. Just believe in yourself.”
But that is not what Exodus teaches.
Moses did not have everything he needed in himself.
He needed the Lord.
He needed God's instruction.
He needed God's presence.
He needed God's power.
And so do we.
The question “What is that in your hand?” is not an invitation to worship our own potential.
It is an invitation to recognize that nothing is too ordinary for God to use according to His purposes.
And sometimes, what He asks us to place at His disposal is not impressive at all.
Maybe it is your ability to listen to someone who is hurting.
Maybe it is the little time you have left after a long day.
Maybe it is your willingness to pray when nobody else knows you are praying.
Maybe it is your experience of suffering, which has taught you to sit beside someone else's pain without offering empty answers.
Maybe it is a gift you have neglected because you keep comparing it with someone else's.
Maybe it is a small opportunity to tell the truth, make restitution, ask forgiveness, or serve someone who cannot repay you.
You may be waiting for something spectacular.
But faithfulness often begins with obedience in what is already before you.
Not because the ordinary is secretly powerful.
But because God is not limited by what looks ordinary to us.
And there's something else in this story that makes it even more personal.
Moses wasn't merely worried about his equipment.
He was worried about himself.
After the signs God gave him, Moses still protested:
“O my Lord, I am not eloquent...” (Exodus 4:10, KJV)
He spoke of being slow of speech and tongue.
And God answered:
“Who hath made man's mouth?” (Exodus 4:11, KJV)
Then came another promise:
“Now therefore go, and I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt say.” (Exodus 4:12, KJV)
Can you imagine standing there?
The Creator of the human mouth was addressing a man who felt unable to speak.
Moses saw a limitation.
God reminded him who was speaking.
But the passage is not telling us that weaknesses do not matter or that faithful people never need help.
In fact, when Moses continued to resist, God was angry, and He appointed Aaron to assist him.
The account is remarkably honest.
Moses hesitated.
Moses objected.
Moses needed help.
And God's purpose still moved forward.
Somebody reading this needs to hear that without twisting it into an excuse for disobedience.
Your weaknesses are real.
Your responsibilities are real.
Your need for wisdom, preparation, community, and accountability is real.
But your limitations do not make God less powerful.
And your fear does not have to be the final voice in your life.
Perhaps you have been calling yourself disqualified because of something that happened years ago.
Perhaps you've been hiding behind a failure that Jesus has been calling you to bring into the light.
Perhaps you've mistaken your current season for your permanent identity.
But Moses reminds us that a person's past does not give us the authority to declare what God can never do with that person's future.
That does not erase the seriousness of sin.
Moses' killing of the Egyptian was not something to celebrate.
God's grace never requires us to rename evil as good.
But Scripture shows us that the Lord can work through deeply imperfect people without approving everything they have done.
And that truth points us toward someone far greater than Moses.
Jesus Christ.
Because the deepest problem in our lives is not that we lack a staff, a platform, a talent, or an opportunity.
It is that we are sinners in need of reconciliation with a holy God.
We need more than inspiration.
We need redemption.
And no amount of personal potential can purchase it.
This is where the story becomes even more beautiful when read within the whole testimony of Scripture.
Moses was sent by God to lead Israel out of physical slavery in Egypt.
That deliverance was a real historical act of God's mercy and covenant faithfulness.
Centuries later, the New Testament reveals Jesus as the One who brings a greater deliverance through His death and resurrection.
Not merely freedom from an earthly ruler.
But forgiveness of sins and liberation from the dominion of sin.
Jesus said:
“If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.” (John 8:36, KJV)
And Hebrews 3:5–6 makes an important distinction.
Moses was faithful as a servant in God's house.
Christ is faithful as the Son over God's house.
Moses matters.
But Jesus is greater.
Moses was a messenger of deliverance.
Jesus is the Savior who accomplished our redemption.
Moses carried a staff in his hand.
Jesus bore a cross on His way to Calvary.
And while the staff in Exodus was a sign through which God displayed His authority, the cross was the place where Christ willingly gave Himself for our sins.
These are not interchangeable objects or identical events.
But they lead us to behold the same sovereign God, whose saving purposes unfold throughout Scripture and reach their fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
Think about the cross for a moment.
To the watching world, crucifixion looked like defeat.
Humiliation.
Shame.
A public scandal.
The Son of God was mocked, rejected, and condemned.
Yet Scripture declares that through His death and resurrection, Jesus accomplished the salvation that sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
Paul wrote:
“For the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God.” (1 Corinthians 1:18, KJV)
And there is a Greek word in that verse worth noticing.
δύναμις — dynamis
It means power.
Not the power of human reputation.
Not the power of religious performance.
Not the power of pretending to be righteous.
The power of God.
The cross announces that our hope is not found in becoming impressive enough for heaven.
Our hope is found in the crucified and risen Christ.
And this is why the Gospel is so different from a motivational speech.
A motivational speech may tell you that you are stronger than you think.
The Gospel tells you that Christ is a mighty Savior, even when you are weak.
A motivational speech may tell you to overcome your past.
The Gospel tells you that sin must be confessed and forsaken, and that forgiveness is found through Jesus Christ.
A motivational speech may tell you to write your own destiny.
The Gospel calls you to repent, believe, and follow the One who gave His life and rose again.
And that brings us to something painfully personal.
What if the question you need to face today isn't merely, “What is in my hand?”
What if it is also:
“What am I refusing to surrender?”
Because sometimes our hands are full.
Full of resentment.
Full of the need to control everything.
Full of excuses.
Full of secret compromises.
Full of bitterness toward someone who hurt us.
Full of ambitions we have never honestly submitted to God.
We ask the Lord to use our lives while refusing to let His Word confront the things destroying them.
We want the comfort of His promises without the inconvenience of obedience.
We want restoration without repentance.
We want the crown without the cross.
But Jesus did not call us to a life of religious appearance.
He called us to follow Him.
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.” (Luke 9:23, KJV)
That is not a call to earn salvation through suffering.
It is a call to a life of surrendered discipleship flowing from faith in Christ.
And surrender is not always dramatic.
Sometimes it happens when you close the browser window you know you shouldn't have opened.
When you tell the truth even though a lie would protect your image.
When you apologize without adding excuses.
When you stop using your pain as permission to wound other people.
When you choose to forgive rather than rehearse revenge.
When you open your Bible after weeks of avoiding it because you know God is calling you back.
When you whisper, through tears, “Lord Jesus, I need You.”
Nobody may applaud that moment.
But obedience is not made valuable by an audience.
It matters because the Lord is worthy.
And perhaps this is where Moses' staff becomes such a powerful reminder.
Later in Exodus, that same staff appears in the unfolding story of Israel's deliverance.
In Exodus 4:20, it is called “the rod of God.”
The staff had not become a god.
It remained an instrument.
But it was now associated with the work God had commanded Moses to undertake.
In Exodus 7, the staff is involved in signs before Pharaoh.
In Exodus 14, Moses is commanded to lift his staff and stretch out his hand over the sea as God makes a way for Israel.
And in Exodus 17, Moses stands with the staff of God in his hand as Israel battles Amalek.
Again and again, the focus is not on the inherent power of the staff.
It is on the faithfulness and authority of the Lord.
The God who called Moses was the God who delivered Israel.
The God who made promises was the God who kept them.
And when we remember that, we stop treating faith like a technique for getting God to fulfill our personal ambitions.
Faith is trust in the God who has revealed Himself.
Even when obedience is difficult.
Even when the outcome is not what we expected.
Even when the wilderness lasts longer than we hoped.
Because here's something we often forget when we celebrate Moses' story.
Moses did not get everything he wanted.
He experienced opposition, exhaustion, criticism, and painful consequences.
He would lead Israel for decades, but he would not personally enter the Promised Land.
His calling was never a guarantee of an easy life.
And ours isn't either.
God can use your gifts without making you famous.
He can make you faithful without making you wealthy.
He can answer your prayers differently from what you imagined.
He can call you to serve quietly, love sacrificially, and endure patiently.
And none of that means your life is wasted.
The greatest evidence of God's love is not that every earthly door opens for us.
It is that while we were sinners, Christ died for us.
Romans 5:8.
Read that truth slowly.
Christ did not wait for you to become impressive.
He did not wait for you to build a reputation.
He did not wait for you to erase your own guilt.
He came to save sinners.
And if you are in Christ, your life is not defined by the worst thing you have done.
It is not defined by the cruelest thing someone has said about you.
It is not defined by the season in which you failed.
Your identity is grounded in the grace of the Savior who died and rose again.
Paul wrote:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17, KJV)
The Greek expression καινὴ κτίσις — kainē ktisis means “new creation.”
That is stronger than a temporary emotional uplift.
Stronger than a new image.
Stronger than changing your public reputation.
It speaks of the transforming reality of belonging to Christ.
And no, becoming a new creation does not mean every painful memory disappears overnight.
It does not mean temptation vanishes.
It does not mean there will be no more tears.
But it does mean that sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to the risen Savior.
Jesus does.
And maybe this is the part of the story you needed most.
You have been so focused on what you lost that you have stopped noticing what remains.
You lost a relationship.
You lost an opportunity.
You lost years you cannot recover.
You lost confidence in yourself.
Perhaps you even lost the respect of people whose approval once meant everything to you.
And now you are standing in the wilderness, wondering whether anything good can still come from your life.
I cannot promise that everything you lost will be returned.
Scripture does not give us permission to make that promise.
But I can point you to a Savior who receives repentant sinners, gives grace to the humble, and calls His people to walk in the good works He has prepared for them.
Ephesians 2:8–10 tells us that salvation is by grace through faith, not by our works, and that those saved by grace are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Notice the order.
We are not saved because we become useful.
We are saved by grace.
And that grace produces a transformed life.
You do not have to purchase God's acceptance by becoming extraordinary.
You come to Jesus in repentance and faith.
And you learn to walk with Him, one act of obedience at a time.
So perhaps tonight, instead of asking God to make you look more like someone else, you could ask Him to make you faithful with what He has entrusted to you.
That conversation you've been avoiding.
That person who needs compassion.
That family member who needs your presence more than your money.
That responsibility you keep postponing.
That sin you need to confess.
That opportunity to share the Gospel with someone who has never truly understood it.
That small act of generosity no one else will notice.
Not every calling looks like Moses standing before Pharaoh.
Some callings look like a father praying with his children.
A mother remaining faithful through exhaustion.
A young believer refusing to compromise.
A widow encouraging another grieving soul.
A worker choosing integrity when dishonesty would be profitable.
A person who has been forgiven by Christ humbly telling someone else where forgiveness can be found.
These things may never make headlines.
But God sees what people overlook.
And there is a world of difference between doing ordinary things to prove our worth and doing them because Christ is worthy.
One leaves us exhausted, always trying to become enough.
The other teaches us to live from the grace we have received.
Now I want to ask you something.
Not as a slogan.
Not as another inspirational line to forget tomorrow.
As a question to carry into prayer.
What is in your hand right now?
Not what you wish you had.
Not what somebody else possesses.
Not what you might have five years from now.
What has God actually entrusted to you today?
And are you willing to obey Him with it?
Perhaps the answer will not come immediately.
Perhaps you need to seek counsel, study Scripture, repent of a sin, or wait patiently for wisdom.
That is okay.
The point is not to manufacture a dramatic calling.
The point is to become attentive to the Lord who has already spoken through His Word.
Because Moses' story is not ultimately about an extraordinary man holding an extraordinary stick.
It is about the extraordinary God who keeps His promises.
And that same God has revealed His saving grace to us in Jesus Christ.
If this story has uncovered something in your heart, don't rush past it.
Maybe you've been hiding behind the words “I'm not enough.”
Maybe you've been clinging to shame that you need to bring before the cross.
Maybe you've been waiting for perfect circumstances before taking the next faithful step.
Maybe you've drifted so far from prayer that you hardly know how to begin again.
Begin here.

“Lord Jesus, I have nothing to boast about before You. I need Your mercy. Forgive my sins. Teach me to trust Your Word, surrender my will, and follow You faithfully. Whatever You have entrusted to me, help me use it for Your glory. And where I have been hiding, lead me into the light. Amen.”
Not because writing those words earns a blessing.
Not because a comment can purchase God's attention.
But because sometimes a simple, honest confession can encourage another struggling believer to stop hiding too.
If you've been learning to follow Christ after a season of failure, share what His grace has been teaching you.
You never know who may read your testimony and find courage to seek the Lord.
And please, don't keep this message only to yourself.
There is also something deeply practical I want to share with you.
Behind every article, every devotional, every biblical resource, and every effort to reach another soul with the Gospel, there is real work.
Writing. Research. Teaching. Preparing resources. Maintaining a growing library.
That work needs prayer.
It needs faithful people willing to share.
And, as resources allow, it needs financial support.
Our desire is to keep making biblical nourishment accessible, especially to those who need encouragement and cannot afford to purchase Christian resources.
And I want to be careful about something important.
Scripture teaches us to give willingly, thoughtfully, and cheerfully, not under pressure or spiritual manipulation (2 Corinthians 9:7).
You can glorify Him through obedience, prayer, faithful service, sharing the Gospel, caring for your family, and generosity according to your means.
It is a voluntary ministry offering, given from gratitude rather than guilt.
Not because spiritual blessings are for sale.
But simply as a gesture of appreciation for those helping sustain the work.
The Gospel is not behind a paywall.
Jesus Christ is not a product.
The message of salvation remains the same for everyone:
Repent and believe the Gospel.
Jesus Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures. He was buried. And He rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
That is the message worth carrying to the world.
That is the truth worth giving our time, talents, and resources to proclaim.
And that is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to make ordinary people feel extraordinary for a moment.
But to point ordinary, broken, sinful, weary people to the extraordinary Savior who makes all things new.
Now return, just for a moment, to the wilderness.
Imagine Moses standing there.
A shepherd.
A fugitive.
An aging man with more questions than confidence.
He has a staff in his hand.
And the Lord asks:
“What is that in your hand?”
Moses could not yet see Pharaoh's palace.
He could not yet see the plagues.
He could not yet see the sea divided.
He could not yet see a nation walking out of bondage.
He could only see what was in front of him.
And he had to respond to the God who was speaking.
Maybe that is where you are tonight.
You cannot see the next ten years.
You cannot undo the last ten.
You cannot control what people will think.
You cannot guarantee that the next step will be easy.
But you can turn to Christ.
You can trust His Word.
You can repent where repentance is needed.
You can obey in the responsibility before you.
And you can stop measuring the worth of your life by how impressive it appears to others.
Because your hope is not that you will someday become another Moses.
Your hope is that you belong to Jesus Christ, the greater Deliverer.
The One who stepped into our broken world.
The One who bore our sins.
The One who conquered death.
The One who welcomes repentant sinners and transforms lives by grace.
So bring Him your fear.
Bring Him your failures.
Bring Him the gifts you have neglected and the excuses you have rehearsed.
Bring Him the truth about yourself.
And trust Him with the next step.
You may be holding something ordinary.
But you are invited to trust a God who is anything but ordinary.
The greatest miracle was never what Moses held in his hand—it was the faithful God who refused to abandon His promise.
